speaker_role: former admissions director (Swarthmore) and former Vanderbilt officer, per his own statement
commercial_incentive: Sells a paid application-review service and promotes it in the video.
key_insights: In committee-based evaluation two officers read one file together: a 'driver' handles the academic side and a 'passenger' handles the student-voice material like essays and activities.
The pair produce ratings and short notes aimed at guiding the later committee about where to look, rather than a final decision.
Colleges adopted this because application volume per officer surged, causing burnout; it cut reading per file while adding a second set of eyes.
Traditional solo reading gave each file 15 to 20 minutes with long comments that were often never reread.
He argues holistic means contextual rather than slow, and that two readers talking in real time catch nuance and reduce individual bias.
In the mock read, ratings are given for academics, activities and major fit, and flags (arts, personal qualities) are added to help the file in final committee.
Region and school-group context, such as how many students from a school were admitted before, is discussed during the read.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Hoffman: two-person reads take about 4 to 8 minutes at many highly selective schools; he cites Bucknell at 6 to 8 minutes.
Hoffman: at Swarthmore reading went from 4-5 applications per hour to about 15 after adopting the model.
Hoffman citing media reports: Georgia Tech reading teams handle about 500 applications a day.
Hoffman: applications per officer doubled during his seven years at Swarthmore; at Vanderbilt he used the traditional model from 2009 to 2015.
Hoffman (mock read): target of roughly 35 files a morning, about 12 per hour.
notable_or_distinctive: Includes a scripted mock two-person read showing ratings, roles and pacing in practice.
reliability_notes: The mock read is fictitious and the speaker notes the model is not universal; the review-service pitch frames the message.
